title: Humphrey’s Executor v. United States
lead: President Roosevelt wanted an FTC commissioner who shared his policy outlook. After the removed commissioner died, his executor’s salary claim asked whether Congress had protected the term and whether that protection was constitutional.

actors.name: William E. Humphrey
actors.role: Federal Trade Commission commissioner with a term ending September 25, 1938; died February 14, 1934.

actors.name: President Franklin Roosevelt
actors.role: Requested resignation and attempted removal for policy and administrative differences, without alleging statutory cause.

actors.name: Humphrey’s executor
actors.role: Sued the United States for salary from October 8, 1933 through Humphrey’s death; docketed as Rathbun, Executor.

actors.name: United States
actors.role: Defended presidential removal in the Court of Claims salary action.

proceedings: Executor filed salary claim in the Court of Claims.
Court of Claims certified whether the statute limited removal and whether that limitation was constitutional.
Supreme Court on May 27, 1935 unanimously answered both questions yes; further disposition remained with the Court of Claims.
limits: The Supreme Court answered certified questions; it did not calculate damages, order reinstatement, or reverse an ordinary lower-court merits judgment. No statutory cause was alleged. Its functional classification and reservations describe the 1935 decision, not all current removal law.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Congress designs a commission with protected terms
paragraphs: Congress created the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) as a five-member body, with no more than three commissioners from one political party, staggered initial terms, and seven-year successor terms. Commissioners could not hold other business or employment, and the Commission selected its own chairman. The statute allowed presidential removal for inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office.

In December 1931, President Hoover nominated William E. Humphrey to succeed himself as commissioner, and the Senate confirmed him. His commission ran through September 25, 1938. The dispute would concern premature removal from that valid appointment, not expiration of the term or a defect in confirmation.

The FTC investigated unfair competition, held notice-and-hearing proceedings, made findings, and issued cease-and-desist orders subject to judicial enforcement and review. It also investigated and reported to Congress and could assist courts as a master in antitrust equity matters. The Supreme Court would characterize those statutory responsibilities as predominantly quasi-legislative and quasi-judicial; that characterization belonged to the particular Commission analyzed in 1935.

sections.title: Roosevelt seeks an official aligned with his administration
sections.cue: Did the President claim inefficiency, neglect, or misconduct?
paragraphs: In July 1933, President Franklin Roosevelt asked Humphrey to resign, saying the Administration’s objectives would be served more effectively by his own personnel choices while disclaiming criticism of Humphrey’s personal service. In August, Roosevelt cited policy and administrative differences and a desire for confidence in the official. Humphrey refused to resign.

On October 7, Roosevelt notified Humphrey that he was removed effective that day. The government did not assert any of the statute’s three causes. Humphrey continued claiming commission membership and entitlement to his $10,000 annual salary, but died on February 14, 1934.

His executor then pursued compensation from October 8, 1933 to death in the Court of Claims. The United States, rather than the President personally, was the defendant. A deceased commissioner’s estate sought unpaid salary, not a judicial order restoring a living officer.

sections.title: The Court of Claims separates two legal questions
sections.cue: Why did statutory construction come before constitutional authority?
paragraphs: The Court of Claims certified whether the FTC Act restricted removal to the enumerated grounds and, if so, whether that restriction was constitutional. The Supreme Court’s task was to answer those questions for the salary action, not review a completed injunction against the President.

The government first argued that listing causes did not eliminate an otherwise unrestricted removal power. Alternatively, it claimed that Article II prevented Congress from imposing that limit. Justice Sutherland’s opinion addressed the statute first: without a restriction actually enacted, there would be no constitutional conflict to resolve.

sources.pinpoint: Procedural history and reasoning; 295 U.S. at 618–23

sections.title: Sutherland reads the fixed term and causes together
sections.cue: Why did Shurtleff not control this statute?
paragraphs: The government relied on Shurtleff, which involved comparable listed removal grounds for a general appraiser but no fixed term. Treating those grounds as exclusive there could effectively confer life tenure absent specified cause; that unusual consequence required clearer legislative direction.

Humphrey’s statute expressly supplied a definite term. A fixed term combined with designated early-removal causes ordinarily protects the term unless another provision or circumstance points elsewhere. Language allowing initial commissioners to continue in office reinforced protection, and the Court saw no reason to protect initial members while denying equivalent protection to successors in the same scheme.

The institutional design confirmed the reading. Long staggered terms, partisan limits, and adjudicatory and advisory duties favored experienced members exercising impartial expert judgment. Reports and debates illuminated that objective, while the Court acknowledged the limits of legislative debate in defining words. At-will removal would undermine the practical assurance: an officer dependent on another’s pleasure would tend to follow that person’s wishes even without formal commands. The term therefore was more than a maximum duration subject to unrestricted shortening.

sections.title: The Court confines Myers to its executive postmaster
sections.cue: Why could Congress protect this commissionership?
paragraphs: For its constitutional defense, the government invoked Myers, which had upheld removal of a first-class postmaster despite a statutory Senate-consent requirement. Sutherland retained Myers’s holding for the purely executive office there but rejected its broader language as controlling all civil officers. Statements exceeding that issue were expressly disapproved insofar as inconsistent with the present result.

The FTC’s responsibilities, as the Court understood them, implicated legislative and judicial work. Applying competition standards resembled legislation and adjudication; reports assisted Congress; service as a master assisted courts. The Commission could perform those functions without executive permission. Incidental executive tasks, including presidentially directed investigations, were treated as ancillary rather than defining the institution.

On that view, separation of powers supported independence. Congress could provide an agency exercising independent judgment to implement legislative policy and assist judicial functions, with tenure protection incident to that design. At-will dismissal would permit indirect presidential control of functions the Court did not classify as the President’s own work. The government’s theory also threatened institutions such as the Interstate Commerce Commission and legislative Court of Claims.

The 1789 debate emphasized in Myers concerned a department whose principal officer answered directly to the President. Historical treatment of officials with judicial responsibilities supported distinguishing this office rather than deriving a universal rule from that debate. The Court reserved positions in the uncertain space between a purely executive officer and this kind of commissionership. It did not resolve every mixed-function agency or every cause provision.

sources.pinpoint: Constitutional reasoning; 295 U.S. at 626–32 & p.628 n.*

sections.title: Both certified answers favor the executor, but no award is calculated
sections.cue: What did unanimity and the McReynolds statement mean?
paragraphs: After argument on May 1, the Supreme Court answered both certified questions “Yes” on May 27, 1935. The Act restricted early removal to inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance, and that restriction was constitutional for this officer. With none of those grounds alleged, the policy-based removal could not be sustained on the government’s theories. The Court of Claims retained responsibility for further disposition of salary.

All Justices agreed with the answers. No separately filed concurrence or dissent appears. A statement recorded Justice McReynolds’s agreement and referred readers to his earlier Myers dissent for his removal views; it was not a newly filed separate opinion here.

The report contains no reinstatement order or computed dollar award and does not decide procedures for a genuinely disputed allegation of statutory cause. Its analysis requires first identifying the protection enacted and then examining its constitutional validity for the office. The label “independent agency” alone does not perform either inquiry. Later powers and modern removal disputes require their own analysis; the source ends with these certified answers.

sources.pinpoint: Judgment, separate-opinion statement, and limits; 295 U.S. at 618–19, 626, 631–32
